implementation_notes: TypeScript layers compile-time checking onto the options object: declare an `Options` interface with optional properties plus defaults, then destructure it in the signature (`function createServer({ port = 8080 }: ServerOptions = {})`) so a typo or a wrong type is a compile error and adding an optional property stays non-breaking. `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` (TS 4.4) makes an optional property mean 'absent or the declared type' instead of 'possibly undefined', `satisfies` keeps literal types when defining default option sets, and `Partial<T>` supports the merge-with-defaults style used when options are layered or come from data. The variants split on where defaults live: per property in the destructuring, or in a merged defaults object.
pitfalls: Defaulting the whole parameter object (`opts: ServerOptions = { host: 'localhost' }`) instead of each property means any partial object replaces all defaults; keep defaults in the destructuring.
Without `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, an optional property implicitly accepts `undefined`, so `{ port: undefined }` compiles and blanks the runtime default unless the code uses `??`.
Structural typing accepts objects with extra keys when they are not fresh literals, so options assembled in a variable can carry typos past the compiler; validate or narrow at the boundary.
`= {}` is still required for no-argument calls: TypeScript checks the signature but cannot stop the runtime destructuring error.

variants.name: Typed defaults merged with Partial<T> overrides
variants.implementation_notes: Keep a canonical defaults object of type `Required<ServerOptions>` and merge a `Partial<ServerOptions>` override into it: `{ ...defaults, ...overrides }`. The merged configuration is a plain data value that can be logged, diffed or persisted, and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` keeps 'absent' and 'undefined' distinct; a helper factory centralises the merge so every entry point applies the same defaults and validation. Choose it when options are layered (file plus flags plus call-site overrides) or serialized; the destructured form remains simpler for direct calls.
pitfalls: The spread is shallow, and `Required<T>` silently stops matching the interface if the interface gains a property with a non-inferable default; keep the defaults object literal typed against the interface (or `satisfies`) so drift is caught.
`Partial<T>` permits `undefined` values that override the default at runtime unless `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is enabled and the merge strips them.
Layered merges make it hard to tell which layer supplied a value; record the source or log the resolved configuration when configuration bugs are costly.
